title: Feel the Page Turn: Read a Graphic Novel for Its Rhythm
subtitle: A short, companionable close-reading exercise for noticing how panels, gutters and page turns shape the pace of a story.
imageAlt: Two friends sit together on a sofa, sharing an open graphic novel and tracing the sequence of panels across a page.
imageConcept: A warm, lived-in living room in late-afternoon light: two friends sit shoulder to shoulder with a graphic novel open between them, one gently pointing to a broad panel while the other looks across the page; show the book’s panel shapes and negative space without legible text.
body: The page is doing more than carrying the plot

A graphic novel can be read quickly for what happens next. But the page itself is also arranging time: a row of small panels may make an action feel incremental, while one broad image can ask the eye to stay a little longer. The distinction is easy to miss when attention is fixed on dialogue and events. It becomes easier when you return to a short sequence and ask not only what happened, but how the page guided you through it.

That shift is the premise of this simple exercise for two people. Choose a sequence of a few pages, read it once without stopping, then go back and look at its visual choices. There is no hidden answer to uncover and no need for specialist vocabulary. The aim is to make the act of reading a little more attentive—and, if you are reading together, to notice whether the page gives each person the same cues or invites different responses. Scholarship on graphic novels treats layout as a central part of the form, alongside style and the relationship between words and images [1].
Start with a sequence that gives you room

Pick a passage short enough to revisit without turning the exercise into homework: a page with a clear change of scene, a brief exchange, a walk, a pause, or a small action. It can be from a book you already know or one neither of you has read. If you are sharing a physical book, sit where both people can see the whole page. With a digital edition, make sure you can move between pages easily and zoom without losing the overall layout.

Agree on a modest boundary before you start: perhaps three pages, or one complete scene. Avoid choosing a passage that depends on context neither reader has; if the sequence feels confusing, simply choose another. The point is not to test comprehension or rank books. It is to give your attention a specific place to land. Keep a scrap of paper nearby if you like, but do not take notes yet. First, let the sequence work at its ordinary reading speed.

On the first pass, read normally. Follow the panels in the order that feels natural, take in the words and pictures, and let the page turn when it comes. Resist the urge to stop and explain a choice. This pass gives each of you a felt sense of the sequence before analysis begins: perhaps it seemed brisk, suspended, funny, tense, or simply clear. Those are starting impressions, not judgments to defend.

When you reach the end, take a moment before talking. Each person can offer one plain observation: “That went faster than I expected,” “I lingered on the last image,” or “I’m not sure when the scene changed.” You do not need to agree. A difference can be useful, but it is not a contest over who read correctly. Panels can function as units of time, with gutters—the spaces between panels—marking the transitions a reader crosses; that basic vocabulary can help describe what you noticed without turning the conversation into a quiz [2].
Return to the page, not just the memory

Now revisit the same sequence, moving slowly enough to see how it is built. Begin with what is observable: how many panels are on each page; whether they are similar in size; where the largest image sits; whether borders are straight, broken, or absent; and how much open space appears between frames. Notice where the dialogue is placed and whether the image seems to confirm, complicate, or contradict the words. You can point to a feature without deciding immediately what it means.

This order matters. In an article about reading visual texts, Nathan C. Phillips describes close looking that begins with features such as framing, color, layout and panel count before asking how those decisions communicate [3]. For a relaxed reading, that can be as simple as saying, “The panels get smaller here,” before adding, “That made the exchange feel quicker to me.” Description gives both readers something concrete to discuss; interpretation can follow, and it can remain tentative.

Scan the sequence for places where the visual rhythm changes. A run of similarly sized panels may create a steady beat; a sudden wide image may interrupt that beat or give a moment room to register. Several small panels can break one action into steps, while a page with fewer, larger images may invite slower looking. These are possibilities, not fixed rules. The effect depends on what is shown, how the images relate, and what each reader brings to the page.

Try asking a few focused questions: Where did your eyes move quickly? Where did they stop? Is there a panel that seems to hold a moment longer than the action itself would take? Did a shift in panel size make you expect a change? Then check the page rather than relying only on memory. In a discussion of the graphic narrative, Raymond Malewitz explains panels as units of time and gutters as the spaces between them, while noting that panel choices can shape visual meaning [2]. That offers a useful lens: the space between images is part of the reading, too.
Treat the gutter as an invitation, not a gap to fill

A gutter is visible space, but what passes through it is often left for the reader to connect. Between two panels, time may have moved forward, an action may have been completed, or the scene may have shifted. Sometimes the transition feels obvious; sometimes the page leaves more uncertainty. Look at one pair of neighboring panels and ask: What changes from the first to the second? What do I infer happened in between? What detail makes that inference feel plausible?

Keep the question open. The goal is not to reconstruct every off-panel event or force a single explanation. You might notice that one reader fills a transition quickly while the other is more aware of what the page does not show. That difference can point back to an observable choice: perhaps a changed background, a shift in expression, or the amount of time implied by the new image. If there is no clear clue, “the page leaves this open” is a complete observation. Not every blank space needs to become a puzzle.
Let the page turn do some of the pacing

A page turn can delay information or reveal a new image all at once. If your chosen sequence includes one, pause before turning back: what did the previous page lead you to expect? What did the next page actually show? Even when the turn reveals nothing dramatic, it may still create a small interval in the reading. On a screen, the equivalent may be moving to the next page or panel; the format changes the gesture, but you can still notice when new information arrives.

For a second pass, compare the page’s layout with the experience you had on the first. Did a large image hold your attention, or did you move past it? Did dialogue make you read the page in a different order from the one you first assumed? Were you carried forward by repeated shapes or stopped by an abrupt change? Baetens and Frey’s discussion of panel and page layout places those design decisions among the central elements of graphic-novel analysis [1]. Here, that idea becomes a practical prompt: notice what the page asks your eyes to do, then see whether that matches what you felt.

Close the exercise with a small exchange rather than a verdict. Each person chooses one moment and finishes the sentence, “The page slowed down for me when…” or “I moved quickly through…” Point to the panel or transition that prompted the response. If the other person saw it differently, ask what they noticed on the page; do not try to settle which reaction is correct. The discussion is about how a design choice worked for each reader, not whether either reader is sufficiently perceptive.

If you want to carry the practice into another reading, keep the same two passes and change just one focus: panel size, the gutter, color, framing, or the page turn. You can do it with a friend, partner, family member, or alone by jotting down one concrete detail after the second pass. The exercise is an editorial invitation to look closely, not a claim that close reading has a particular guaranteed effect. A few minutes is enough to make the page’s rhythm visible—and to leave the story intact.
